label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's a draft you can post as-is. I've kept it anonymous, kept the argument on the numbers rather than the politics, and included a policy skeleton Brenda can lift straight into the 18th.

---

Peter, thanks for putting your hand to it plainly. Nine years running payroll isn't guessing, and I'd rather take your argument seriously than treat it as a Finance line to be argued with. You're right about more than most people in this thread will give you credit for.

I want to push back on one part, but the reason I think it's worth your attention — and Brenda's — is that we actually ran your experiment. February 2025. We closed the window, gave two months' notice, ran a financial literacy session with the SACCO, pointed people at SACCOs and banks. Almost the same argument, very nearly the same words.

Then we watched what happened.

**The need doesn't go away, it just changes where it lands.**

We're a transport and warehousing operation, about 340 staff, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. In the six months after we closed the window, debt collector and loan app calls to our office went from a handful to 61 logged by reception. Some of those apps were calling our supervisors directly, listed as "referees" on the loan. That puts our people in a considerably worse position than a payroll advance ever did — a referee on a 30% app is a person who gets chased, and who then has to explain to their family why their name is on it.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end went up, and our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were "sorting out" loans instead of running loads. None of that appears anywhere on a payroll forecast. That's the piece I think is easy to miss from inside a payroll function: the cost doesn't disappear, it moves to where the spreadsheet doesn't look — and it lands on operations, not on Finance.

**It also got worse for the individual, not better.**

SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and need guarantors. Useless for a child sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. We had a loader at one of our Mombasa depots come to us with six apps running at once by the time he reached us — borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind it.

Six apps at once, unwound over four months, is not a better outcome than an advance at a fixed cap. It's the same distress, with more interest and a guarantor.

**What we run now**

We reopened in September 2025, as a written policy:

- **Cap:** maximum 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle
- **Statutory check:** we confirm total deductions stay within the Employment Act's limit of two-thirds of wages before approving, so nobody ends up with nothing at month end
- **Repayment:** deducted in full at the next payroll. No interest, no fee, no extension
- **Route:** request through the payroll portal, not through me or a line supervisor's desk. This is the part that answers your "HR becomes the lender of first resort" point — the request never lands on a human's desk, it's a form with a rule attached
- **Notice and literacy:** two months' notice and a financial literacy session with the SACCO, which we kept and I'd keep again

Since reopening: 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. We recovered 100% except two leavers. Total written off for the year was roughly KES 14,000.

**The arithmetic, which is what actually changed our Finance Manager's mind**

KES 14,000 of write-offs for a year, against the cost of the absence, the missed runs and the staff time that closure created — and that cost sits across departments, not in one line. But the bigger point is this: our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself, because the forecast impact is known in advance. It's a fixed ceiling, not a surprise. The objection was never really cash flow. It was not knowing what was coming.

**Where I think you're right, and I'd say so to my own MD**

- The informal version is genuinely bad. We had one. No written limit, no rule, supervisor's discretion. Some people took it literally every month and your Finance colleague is right about that. Brenda's Finance Manager will be right about it too. That's an argument for writing rules down, not for closing the window.
- Recovery when someone leaves is real. Two leavers, roughly KES 14,000. Small, but small is not zero.
- HR time is real. We solved that with the portal route rather than by removing the scheme.
- Advances can teach people to live on next month's money — but only if you let the balance run. Unmanaged was our old scheme. 40% of net, once a cycle, repaid at the next payroll is not a revolving balance. Nobody is funding a lifestyle; they're covering a two-week gap at most.

**What I'd suggest Brenda takes into the 18th**

Not a complaint, and not "can we keep advances somehow." A proposal with the cap, the frequency, the repayment term and the approval route written on one page, so the burden of proof moves from "can this person be trusted" to "does this request meet the policy."

I'd also make the meeting three-way rather than two-way. Bring Finance in on the design, because the design is what made our Finance Manager the scheme's biggest defender. A written ceiling is something a Finance Manager can plan around; an open-ended discretionary arrangement is what actually keeps them awake.

And I'd ask for something specific: not a decision on the 18th, but agreement in principle to a written scheme with these four rules, with the policy drafted in January. If it goes in as "no" versus "here is the cap, the frequency, the repayment and the route", Finance gets a fixed ceiling and Brenda gets a policy she can defend.

For what it's worth, Peter, I don't think we're arguing about whether advances are good. We're arguing about whether a company with a written cap is better than a company with a blank cheque and a loan app. I've run the blank cheque version and I've run the written version, and the written one is the one I'd keep.

Happy to share the reconciliation we did — the write-off figure against absence and missed runs, and the actual policy wording — if either of you want the detail rather than the summary.

---

One thing worth deciding before you post: the reconciliation is the strongest single item, but sharing numbers in detail on a public board can identify a firm even without naming it. If you'd rather keep it general, cut the second-to-last paragraph and offer to share details by direct message instead.
